# Mechanistic Studies and Identification of Catalyst Deactivation Pathways for Pyridine(diimine) Iron Catalyzed C(sp2)–H Borylation

**Authors:** Tianyi Zhang; Tyler P. Pabst; Jordan M. Hoyt; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Paul J. Chirik

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

The synthesis and application of aryl-substituted pyridine(diimine) iron complexes (RPDI)FeCH3 to the catalytic borylation of heteroarenes under thermal conditions is described. Improvements in catalyst design and performance were guided by precatalyst activation studies, where investigations into stoichiometric reactivities of iron borohydride (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(H2BPin) and iron furyl (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(2-methylfuryl) complexes revealed facile C(sp2)–H activation and a slower and potentially turnover-limiting C(sp2)–B formation step. Formation of the flyover dimer, [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe]2 was identified as a catalyst deactivation pathway and formally iron(0) complexes were found to be inactive for borylation. The pyridine(diimine) iron borohydride, flyover dimer and furyl complexes were characterized by X-ray diffraction and their electronic structures determined by a combination of NMR, EPR, and Mössbauer spectroscopies corroborated by DFT calculations. The role of the redox-active pyridine(diimine) ligand in catalytic C–H borylation was also investigated.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

The functionalization of C–H bonds is a step-economical strategy that has been a longstanding challenge in synthetic chemistry.1 Among the various methods, C–H borylation is particularly desirable as the resultant boronic esters are synthetic lynchpins for a host of C–C and C–X bond forming reactions.2 Specifically, iridium-catalyzed C–H borylation, independently developed by Hartwig and Smith,3,4 is one of the most widely applied C–H functionalization methods owing to high activity, predictable sterically driven site selectivity, and functional group compatibility.5 The accepted pathway for iridium-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation with bipyridine-type ligands involves an Ir(III)–Ir(V) redox cycle with turnover-limiting C(sp2)–H oxidative addition from an iridium(III) tris(boryl) resting state (Figure 1a).3b,6

Interest has intensified for the discovery and adoption of catalysts with more earth-abundant metals for C–H functionalization.7,8 The relatively high density of states and access to open shell intermediates with first row transition metals offer the opportunity for distinct reactivity but also poses challenges for developing the fundamental organometallic chemistry to promote the desired transformations.9 In addition to examples of cobalt-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation reported by Driess, Smith and others,10 our group has developed a family of pincer-supported cobalt complexes for the borylation of arenes and heteroarenes (Figure 1b).11 In the cases examined, the experimental and computational data support a Co(I)–Co(III) redox couple where C(sp2)–H oxidative addition occurs from a cobalt(I)-boryl intermediate. The relative rate of the C(sp2)–H activation step compared to others in the cycle is catalyst and substrate dependent. With pincers with phosphine donors, electron-poor substrates such as fluoroarenes undergo fast and reversible C(sp2)–H oxidative addition while for more electron-rich examples such as 2,6-lutidine, C(sp2)–H oxidative addition is turnover limiting.10,12 In addition, the nickel-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation of (hetero)arenes has also been studied by several groups,13 with nickel nanoparticles proposed as the active catalyst in some cases.

Concerns over the toxicity of cobalt and nickel and the sourcing of the former inspire the development of catalysts based on iron.7d,14,15 Despite an initial report by Hartwig and coworkers on stoichiometric, photochemical borylation of C(sp2)–H bonds promoted by CpFe(CO)2–BCat in 1995 (Figure 1c),16 iron-catalyzed C–H borylation remains in the early stages of development with limited mechanistic understanding.17 Under photochemical conditions, Mankad and coworkers reported the heterobimetallic (Cp)(CO)2Fe–Cu-(NHC) catalyst, where catalyst deactivation by Fp2 dimer (Fp = (Cp)(CO)2Fe) formation is circumvented by Fe–Cu bond formation upon H2 elimination.18 Using monometallic bis-(phosphine) iron(II) dimethyl precatalysts, Darcel and coworkers reported arene C(sp2)–H borylation with a proposed mechanism featuring Fe(0)–Fe(II) redox cycling, while Thomas and coworkers demonstrated the viability of in situ catalyst generation from the corresponding bis(phosphine) iron(II) chloride.17

For thermal iron-catalyzed C–H borylation (Figure 1c), Okhi, Tatsumi, and coworkers demonstrated facile C(sp2)–H activation and C–B bond formation mediated by Cp(NHC)Fe alkyl/aryl complexes and identified iron borohydride formation as a catalyst deactivation pathway.17,20 Kamitani and coworkers proposed redox-neutral C–H activation by a putative iron bisalkoxide complex supported by PNN ligands.17 In addition to an off-cycle dimeric iron hydride complex, Nishibayashi and coworkers identified a catalytically active square planar (PNP)FeII–X (X = H, BPin, furyl) complexes (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) capable of C(sp2)–H activation and C–B bond formation at 100 °C.17c,21

To date, iron-catalyzed C–H borylation has been dominated by complexes supported by strong-field ligands such as cyclopentadienyls, phosphines and/or N-heterocyclic carbenes. Alternatives with weaker field, potentially redox-active chelates remain underexplored (Figure 2a). This latter class of iron compounds is attractive given the synthetic and electronic modularity of pyridine(diimine) (PDI) iron complexes,22 the precedent for engaging in bond activation chemistry involving metal–ligand cooperativity,19,23 and distinct redox flexibility.24 In addition, while the mechanism of iridium- and cobalt-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation has been well-studied,6,11 there is limited understanding of how iron catalysts operate. Open questions include the nature and oxidation state of the iron intermediate responsible for C–H activation, the role of redox cycling during catalytic turnover and the origin of catalyst deactivation. Gaining insights into these fundamental processes is essential for increasing both the activity and synthetic utility of iron catalysts for C–H borylation.

Here we describe the synthesis and evaluation of pyridine-(diimine) iron alkyl complexes for the catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation of heteroarenes (Figure 2b). Catalyst deactivation pathways were identified that enabled improvements in catalyst performance. Catalytically active iron intermediates including borohydride (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(H2BPin) and furyl (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(2-methylfuryl) complexes were identified as well as the off-cycle, flyover dimer, [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe]2 by a combination of X-ray diffraction, NMR, EPR, and Mössbauer spectroscopies. Stoichiometric studies were used to establish key elementary organometallic steps as well as the identification of the resting state and the turnover limiting step.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Initial Evaluation of the Reactivity of (PDI)FeCH3 Precatalysts in Catalytic C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complex, 1–CH3 was evaluated for the catalytic borylation of 2-methylfuran (6). Standard conditions employed 10 equiv of 6, 1 equiv of HBPin, 5 mol % of the iron methyl complex at 50 °C for 16 h. This procedure generated the 5-borylated furan product (7) in 47% yield as quantified by 1H NMR spectroscopy versus an internal standard (Scheme 1a).

The observation of borylation activity motivated additional investigations into the potential intermediacy of an iron boryl complex and determination of its electronic structure, specifically if there is any involvement of the redox activity of the pyridine(diimine) chelate. Addition of one equivalent of HBPin to a benzene-d6 solution of 1–CH3 resulted in immediate consumption of the organometallic iron complex with concomitant formation of methane as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Scheme 1b). Monitoring the reaction over time produced new resonances signaling gradual formation of a pyridine(diimine) iron dinitrogen complex, assigned as 5–(N2)2 where the 4-position of the pyridine ring has undergone C–H borylation. Resubjecting 5–(N2)2 to analogous reaction conditions with 2-methylfuran did not produce any observable borylation.

Based on these observations and the lack of evidence for benzene-d6 borylation by NMR spectroscopy or gas chromatography, a pathway whereby the transfer of the boryl to the pyridine(diimine) ligand was considered. Similar borylation reactivity and deactivation was observed with [(iPrPNP)Co] catalysts (PNP = bisphosphinopyridine).11b A plausible pathway involves reaction of 1–CH3 with HBPin to generate methane along with a transient iron-boryl complex that in turn undergoes intermolecular C(sp2)–H activation at 4-position of the PDI pyridine ring to afford the corresponding iron hydride (5–H). Such reactivity was observed with cobalt pincer borylation catalysts.11b Rapid bimolecular reductive elimination of H2 in the presence of N2 forms the dinitrogen complex 5–(N2)2 (Scheme 1b), analogous to the reactivity of the corresponding pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complexes.24

### Catalytic Performance of 4-Substituted (PDI)Fe Complexes for C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The competing borylation of the 4-position of the pyridine(diimine) ligand prompted the exploration of iron methyl compounds with substituents designed to block ligand modification (Scheme 1c). The catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation with each of the pyridine(diimine)iron methyl complexes was evaluated with 6 as a representative substrate (Table 1). Using bis(pinacolato)-diboron (B2Pin2) as the boron reagent,25 heating 5 mol % of 1–CH3 in neat 6 at 50 °C furnished the 5-borylated product (7) in 47% yield (entry 1). A significant increase in yield to 170% (out of a theoretical maximum of 200%) was observed with 2–CH3 as the precatalyst (entry 2), establishing the impact of the 4-substituent. An 80% yield of 7 was obtained with 2–CH3 and one equivalent of HBPin (entry 5), demonstrating that the HBPin byproduct formed from C(sp2)–H borylation with B2Pin2 is also an effective borylating reagent. This accounts for the theoretical maximum yield of 200% (relative to B2Pin2 equivalence) for borylation with B2Pin2.

Replacing the 4-tert-butyl group on the pyridine of the chelate with a more electron-donating pyrrolidinyl substituent did not lead to significant changes in catalytic performance, as similar yields were observed with 2–CH3 and 3–CH3 using either B2Pin2 (entries 2 and 3) or HBPin (entries 5 and 6) as the boron reagent. This suggests limited opportunities for modifying the electron-donating ability of the pyridine-(diimine) ligand for additional catalyst improvement. Reducing the size of the 2,6-aryl substituents from 2,6-diisopropyl (2–CH3) to 2,6-dimethyl (4–CH3) on the N-imine resulted in a loss of catalytic activity (entries 4 and 7), suggesting that the more sterically accessible iron center results in more rapid deactivation rather than improved performance. These results are consistent with recent findings that larger aryl imine substituents impart greater kinetic stability to (PDI)FeCH3 complexes.24

Pyridine(diimine) iron complexes in the formal iron(0) oxidation state were also investigated as precatalysts for the C(sp2)–H borylation of 6 given their well-precedented catalytic activity.26 The iron bis(dinitrogen) complex, 2–(N2)2 as well as the iron methyl ate complex, [2–CH3]– were evaluated (entries 8 and 9) and no appreciable activity was observed in either case. The results suggest that oxidative addition to formally iron(0) compounds is not operative and also provides insight into the inactivity of the more open iron methyl complexes as these are known to undergo rapid bimolecular elimination of ethane to form formally iron(0) compounds. Attempts to borylate thiophenes, pyrroles, oxazoles and pyridines were unsuccessful, producing only trace quantities of the organoboronate ester.27

### Stoichiometric Reactivity of (4-tBu-iPrPDI)FeCH3 Complexes with Boron Reagents.

The observation of catalytic borylation activity with pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complexes prompted more detailed studies into the mechanism of the reaction. To study activation of the iron precatalyst, a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 was treated with one equivalent of HBPin (Scheme 2). Complete consumption of the iron methyl complex was observed within 5 min and the formation of CH3BPin was confirmed by 1H and 11B NMR spectroscopies. Addition of excess HBPin formed a red-brown solution with paramagnetically broadened and shifted 1H NMR resonances. The iron product was identified as the pyridine(diimine) iron borohydride complex, 2–(H2BPin) based on single-crystal X-ray diffraction (vide infra). 2–(H2BPin) is likely formed by capture of the iron hydride intermediate 2–H by HBPin.

In the absence of excess HBPin, 2–(H2BPin) was consumed with concomitant formation of HBPin, H2 and the reported iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2.28 A separate recrystallization following the treatment of 2–CH3 with one equivalent of HBPin in pentane at −35 °C produced dark green crystals that were identified as the iron flyover dimer, 2–Dimer as determined by X-ray diffraction. Dissolution of 2–Dimer in benzene-d6 under N2 atmosphere led to the formation of 2–(N2)2 as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy, while subjecting 2–(N2)2 to analogous recrystallization conditions did not furnish 2–Dimer, demonstrating irreversible conversion to the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2. In a control experiment, a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(N2)2 was treated with 2 equiv of HBPin at ambient or elevated temperatures and neither the consumption of 2–(N2)2 nor the formation of 2–(H2BPin) was observed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. Similarly, addition of excess HBPin to 2-Dimer at room or elevated temperature did not yield observable quantities of 2-(H2BPin). Notably, activation of C(sp2)–H, B–H, and B–B bonds was sluggish with either 2–Dimer or 2–(N2)2 at both room and elevated temperatures.

Treatment of a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 with 1 equiv of B2Pin2 at ambient temperature resulted in complete consumption of the iron methyl complex within 5 min along with formation of 2–(N2)2, CH3BPin and HBPin. No evidence was obtained for borylation of the solvent. Recrystallization from pentane at −35 °C resulted in isolation of 2–Dimer. It is posited that an iron-boryl complex, 2–BPin is initially formed from the reaction between 2–CH3 and B2Pin2 and in the absence of a suitably activated C(sp2)–H bond, 2–BPin undergoes the loss of boryl as B2Pin2 to form 2–Dimer. One possibility is the ejection of boryl radical though this is unlikely given the relatively strong DFT-computed Fe–B bond of 49.1 kcal/mol (see Scheme S2). In comparison to the isolable, 4-coordinate and idealized planar (PNP)Fe(II) boryl complex (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) reported by Nishibayashi and coworkers,17c the transient nature of the (PDI)Fe–boryl complex supports the role of the strong-field pincer in stabilizing the iron boryl intermediate through stronger Fe to B π-backbonding. Moreover, this is consistent with DFT calculations (Scheme S2) which suggest a substantially weaker Fe–B bond in the 2–BPin intermediate (BDFE = 49.1 kcal/mol) than in Nishibayashi’s (PNP)FeBPin (BDFE = 68.3 kcal/mol). Taken together, the stoichiometric experiments demonstrate that the coordination of HBPin to 2–H is reversible and that the formation of the 2–Dimer is a catalyst deactivation pathway for [(PDI)Fe] class of borylation catalysts.

### Characterization of Pyridine(diimine) Iron Complexes Relevant to Catalytic C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The solid-state structure of (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(κ2–H2BPin) was determined by single crystal X-ray diffraction (Figure 3a) and confirmed the identity of the compound. Two bridging hydrogen atoms were located in the difference map and established the presence of an LX-type borohydride ligand rather than an X-type boryl. The Fe–B bond distance of 2.158(3) Å is significantly longer than the sum of the van der Waals radii of iron and boron (2.05 Å) and those of known iron boryl complexes,17,29 but falls within the range of those in known FeII–H–B complexes (1.855(2) to 2.319(3) Å),30 further supporting the assignment as the iron borohydride.

Notably, the iron borohydride 2–(H2BPin) is related to the cobalt(III) dihydridoboryl complexes, L3Co(H)2(BPin) reported by our laboratory that are precatalysts for C(sp2)–H borylation.31 With iron, the less electron donating and redox-active pyridine(diimine) favors reductive coupling and hence the five-coordinate iron borohydride 2–(H2BPin) and raises the question about the role of redox cycling in catalytic borylation.

To investigate the electronic structure of 2–(H2BPin), the solid-state, zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum was collected and exhibits a single quadrupole doublet with an isomer shift (δ) of 0.29 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 1.54 mm/s (Figure 3b). The DFT computed isomer shift of 0.37 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 1.82 mm/s are in agreement with the experimental data and support a BS(2,1) electronic structure description for 2–(H2BPin), featuring an intermediate-spin Fe center (SFe = 1) with a monoreduced PDI ligand.32 The X-band EPR spectrum was recorded at 10 K and features a rhombic signal with g-values of 2.73, 2.07, 2.02 (Figure 3c), consistent with a metal centered radical in an overall S = 1/2 complex. The spin density plot for the BS(2,1) electronic structure description of 2–(H2BPin) (Figure 3d) revealed spin delocalization on the imine and pyridine portion of the PDI ligand. Thus, the overall S = 1/2 ground state is best described as an intermediate spin iron(II) complex (SFe = 1) engaged in antiferromagnetic coupling with a pyridine-(diimine)-centered radical. While known iron borohydrides are diamagnetic,17,33 2–(H2BPin) represents a rare example of a paramagnetic iron borohydride derivative.

The flyover dimer, 2–Dimer was also characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. In the solid state, overall idealized C2 symmetry was observed between the two iron centers and the supporting pyridine (diimine) ligands (Figure 4a). Each iron center (e.g., Fe1) has one imine N atom (e.g., N4) and one pyridine N atom (N5) coordinated from one PDI ligand, while the imine C=N double bond on the second PDI ligand (e.g., N1 and C13) is η2 coordinated to the same iron center, likely to maximize π-backbonding. Accordingly, the N(1)–C(13) bond is elongated to 1.389(4) Å as compared to the N(4)–C(61) bond length of 1.335(4) Å (Figure 4b). A significant distortion from planarity is also observed around each iron center (τ4′ = 0.462) as each iron atom is raised out of the pincer plane, as evidenced by the bond angles around the iron center. The two iron centers are separated by 4.255 Å, rendering metal–metal bonding unlikely. In benzene-d6, 2–Dimer was NMR silent as no resonances were observed that could be assigned to the compound. This behavior likely arises from magnetic coupling between the two iron centers through the pyridine(diimine) ligands or due to dynamic behavior of the dimer in solution.

Iron hydrides were considered as possibilities for the structure of 2–Dimer. While the paramagnetism of the sample precludes reliable, direct observation by NMR spectroscopy, the lack of reactivity with HBPin, B2Pin2 or 2-methylfuran supports their absence.34 Likewise, no bands diagnostic of Fe–H stretches35 were observed in the infrared spectrum. While circumstantial and principally negative evidence, the combined data supports the formulation as the dimer of [(PDI)Fe].

The zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum of 2–Dimer was recorded in the solid state at 80 K and exhibits an isomer shift of 0.63 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 1.14 mm/s (Figure 4c). The observed isomer shift is consistent with reported values (0.49–0.57 mm/s) for high-spin (S = 2) iron(II) complexes with pyridine(diimine) ligands.24 The observed quadrupole splitting is consistent with the reported value (1.17 mm/s) for a related CS-symmetric dinuclear (PDI)Fe(II) complex formed from the corresponding PDI iron methyl complex by bimolecular reductive elimination of ethane.36 No signal was observed when collecting the X-band EPR spectrum of 2–Dimer in toluene glass at 10 K. Furthermore, the DFT-calculated relative energies, Mössbauer parameters (δ = 0.56 mm/s, |ΔEQ|=0.84 mm/s, Table S1) and metrical parameters suggest that the electronic structure of 2-Dimer is best described as two high-spin (S = 2) Fe(II) centers engaged in antiferromagnetically coupling, corroborating the C2-symmetry observed in the solid-state structure.

### Isolation of Catalytically Relevant Iron Complexes: Identification of Facile C(sp2)–H Activation and Slow C(sp2)–B Bond Formation.

With the identification of the precatalyst activation and catalyst deactivation pathway, the stoichiometric reactivity of pyridine(diimine) iron complexes in C(sp2)–H activation was investigated using 6 as a representative substrate. Addition of one equivalent of B2Pin2 to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 in the presence of 2 equiv of 2-methylfuran at room temperature resulted in the formation of a new paramagnetic product identified as the iron furyl complex, 2–(2-Me)Furyl. The expected organic byproduct, CH3BPin was also observed by NMR spectroscopy (Scheme 3a). Performing a related experiment with one equivalent of HBPin also resulted in clean conversion to 2–(2-Me)Furyl, which was then isolated as dark brown crystals in 91% yield, following recrystallization in a pentane/toluene solution at −35 °C. In contrast, 2–CH3 did not react with 2-methylfuran in the absence of boron reagents at room temperature. Heating a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 to 65 °C for 24 h in the presence of 10 equiv of 2-methylfuran furnished 2–(2-Me)Furyl, demonstrating a lower barrier for C(sp2)–H activation by iron boryls over iron alkyls.

Addition of one equivalent of 2-methylfuran to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(H2BPin) at ambient temperature resulted in clean and quantitative formation of 2–(2-Me)Furyl, consistent with reversible HBPin dissociation from 2–(H2BPin) to generate an intermediate iron hydride 2–H responsible for C(sp2)–H activation (Scheme 3b). In contrast, the iron borohydride, (η5-C5Me5)(NHC)Fe(H2BPin), isolated by Okhi and Tatsumi, contains a substantially shorter Fe–B distance of 2.002(3) Å than the value of 2.158(3) Å in 2–(H2BPin) and is inactive for catalytic borylation (Figure 3a).17a This reactivity difference is likely a result of a higher barrier for HBPin dissociation to generate the active iron hydride, a consequence of stronger π-backbonding from a more electron-rich iron(II) center arising from more electron-donating ligands.

Taken together, the stoichiometric studies demonstrate that C(sp2)–H activation by the pyridine(diimine) iron hydride (2–H) or boryl (2-BPin) has a lower activation barrier than that by the corresponding iron methyl (2–CH3) complex and is more likely to be the dominant pathway under catalytic conditions. Similar trends in relative rates of C(sp2)–H activation have been observed in reported (PNP)Co–X (X = H, alkyl, and BPin) complexes (PNP = bisphosphinopyridine).11

Single-turnover experiments were carried out to determine the catalytic competency of 2–(2-Me)Furyl (Scheme 3c). Addition of one equivalent of B2Pin2 to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(2-Me)Furyl and heating to 50 °C generated the borylated product, 7 in 78% yield. No reaction was observed when the procedure was conducted at ambient temperature. Using HBPin in place of B2Pin2 under analogous conditions produced a similar yield of 71% of 7. Related stoichiometric reactivity was observed for the (PNP)Fe(furyl) complex (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) reported by Nishibayashi and coworkers.17c These results suggest that 2–(2-Me)Furyl is likely on-cycle and catalytically competent. In both cases (B2Pin2 and HBPin), conversion to the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2 was the only observed iron-containing product by 1H NMR spectroscopy, presumably formed from the transiently generated iron boryl (2–BPin) or hydride (2–H) complexes in the absence of excess furan (Scheme 2). Analysis of the results of the stoichiometric studies suggests that with pyridine(diimine) iron complexes, C(sp2)–B formation incurs a higher activation barrier than C(sp2)–H activation and may be the turnover-limiting step (Scheme 3a,b).

The solid-state structure of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and confirms the identity of the molecule as an idealized planar iron complex. An Npyridine–Fe–C angle of 174.44 (14)° is observed and the furanyl ring is rotated by 43° relative to the idealized iron-chelate plane (Figure 5a). The Nimine–Cimine bond distances of 1.326(4) Å and 1.339(4) Å and Cimine–Cipso values of 1.442(4) Å and 1.431(4) Å are consistent with reported values for (PDI)FeX (X = halides, alkyl) and are diagnostic of a monoreduced [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)]1– ligand coordinated to a ferrous center.37

The zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was recorded in the solid state at 80 K and exhibits quadrupole doublets with an isomer shift (δ) of 0.30 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 3.68 mm/s (Figure 5b), consistent with the reported values for analogous idealized planar pyridine(diimine) iron alkyl/aryl complexes including: 2–CH3 (δ = 0.31 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 3.73 mm/s) and (iPrPDI)Fe(2-benzofuryl) (δ = 0.33 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 3.55 mm/s).24,38 2–(N2) and 2–(N2)2 side products formed during synthesis cocrystallized with 2–(2-Me)Furyl and were also identified in the Mössbauer spectrum.28 The band asymmetry observed for 2–(N2)2 is likely due to sample inhomogeneity or overlapping peaks in the mixture. Spectra of the isolated material do not exhibit this asymmetry.28 The X-band EPR spectrum of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was recorded in toluene glass at 10 K and a rhombic signal was observed and simulated to provide g-values of 3.36, 1.90, and 1.85 (Figure 5c). The simulation is most consistent with an overall S = 1/2 complex with iron-centered radical. A near-idealized planar geometry around the iron center and the Mössbauer and EPR data support an intermediate-spin iron(II) center (SFe = 1) engaged in antiferromagnetically coupling to a monoreduced pyridine(diimine) radical anion (SPDI = 1/2). Thus, the overall C(sp2)–H activation reactions from (PDI)Fe–X (X = H, CH3, BPin) are net redox-neutral as both reactants and products have identical electronic structures.

### Proposed Mechanism for (PDI)Fe-Catalyzed C(sp2)–H Borylation.

With the results of the stoichiometric studies in hand, a mechanism for (PDI)Fe-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation was proposed with 6 as a representative substrate and the iron methyl complex 2–CH3 as the precatalyst (Scheme 4). With B2Pin2 as the borylating reagent, activation of 2–CH3 with B2Pin2 forms the putative iron boryl complex 2–BPin. This then undergoes facile C(sp2)–H activation with 2-methylfuran to form the iron furyl complex, 2–(2-Me)Furyl, which is the catalyst resting state. Alternatively, the activation of precatalyst 2–CH3 with HBPin leads to the formation of iron hydride 2–H, which is in equilibrium with the iron borohydride, 2–(H2BPin) in the presence of excess HBPin. Given that HBPin is a byproduct of C(sp2)–H borylation with B2Pin2, both 2–BPin and 2–(H2BPin) are relevant intermediates during catalytic borylation. In the presence of substrate, 2–H also undergoes the C(sp2)–H bond activation with a relatively low barrier to form 2–(2-Me)Furyl. Direct C(sp2)–H activation by 2–CH3 is comparatively sluggish and therefore catalyst initiation is slower than C(sp2)–H bond activation from catalytically active compounds. The isolation of iron(II) borohydride 2–(H2BPin), instead of an iron dihydridoboryl complex analogous to L3CoIII(H)2(BPin),11 suggests that C(sp2)–H activation by (PDI)Fe–X (X = H, CH3, BPin) is less likely to proceed by oxidative addition with Fe(II/III) redox cycling; instead, a redox-neutral mechanism akin to σ-complex-assisted metathesis (σ-CAM) is more plausible.

From the iron furyl complex 2–(2-Me)Furyl, a reaction with B2Pin2 through potentially turnover-limiting C(sp2)–B formation then affords product 7, with the reformation of 2–BPin. Alternatively, 2–(2-Me)Furyl reacts with HBPin to yield product 7 with the regeneration of 2–H (and 2–(H2BPin) when HBPin is in excess). In the absence of excess 6, the competing catalyst deactivation pathway becomes more dominant, where 2–BPin and 2–H undergo the loss of boryl as B2Pin2 and a bimolecular reductive elimination of H2, respectively, to the flyover dimer 2–Dimer and eventually the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2. Both complexes are catalytically inactive and incapable of reentering the catalytic cycle under standard conditions.

In summary, the evaluation of various pyridine(diimine) iron complexes for the catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation of 2-methylfuran and gaining mechanistic insights through stoichiometric experiments and electronic structure studies have provided a foundation for the development of catalyst design principles (Figure 6). Substitution of the 4-position of the pyridine(diimine) ligand boosts catalytic activity by minimizing competing borylation of this site that in turn leads to catalyst deactivation. The size of the 2,6-aryl substituents is also important for maintaining catalyst performance as larger isopropyl groups stabilize the iron complex from deleterious bimolecular reductive elimination. Notably, formally iron(0) complexes supported by pyridine(diimines) were inactive for borylation, arising from the inability of these compounds to activate HBPin or B2Pin2. Overall, these catalyst design principles would hopefully provide the foundation for the design of next generation iron C–H borylation catalysts.

## CONCLUSIONS

Mechanistic investigations into C(sp2)–H borylation of 2-methylfuran catalyzed by (PDI)FeCH3 precatalysts were conducted. Identification of boryl migration upon activation of (iPrPDI)FeCH3 motivated mechanism-guided catalyst design to circumvent the deactivation pathway by ligand modifications. Following the investigation of the stoichiometric reactivity of [(PDI)Fe] complexes with boron reagents and the C(sp2)–H activation of 2-methylfuran, catalytically active as well as off-cycle [(PDI)Fe] complexes were identified, isolated and their solid-state and electronic structures unambiguously determined by X-ray diffraction, NMR, EPR and Mössbauer spectroscopies as well as computational studies. Based on stoichiometric experiments, the formation of a pyridine(diimine) iron flyover-dimer complex was identified as a catalyst deactivation pathway. C(sp2)–H activation by transient pyridine(diimine) iron hydride and iron boryl complexes was faster than with the corresponding iron methyl, and occurs through a net redox-neutral pathway. Idealized planar, intermediate spin ferrous compounds engaged in antiferromagnetic coupling with a chelate radical anion are persistent throughout. Stoichiometric studies support C–B bond formation as having a higher barrier than C(sp2)–H activation and is therefore the likely turnover-limiting step. These findings provide rare insights into a catalytic borylation process with paramagnetic iron compounds and provide the foundation for next generation catalyst design.
